topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; frameworks and competencies may need adaptation for Australian healthcare systems, funding models, and regulatory environment.
takeaways: Identifies core digital competencies needed in public health roles; consider which competencies map to your organisation's AI upskilling priorities and where gaps exist in current staff capability.

European framework may highlight competency areas (e.g., data governance, digital ethics) relevant for designing AI literacy programmes, though local Australian health policy and procurement practices should be checked.
Provides structure for mapping competency levels across roles — useful for segmenting AI training by job function rather than one-size-fits-all approach.

articles.title: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to EU public health systems and digital literacy (not AI-specific). Applicability to Australian healthcare contexts and private sector settings would require careful translation.
takeaways: Use evidence gap analysis frameworks to identify where digital literacy assessments are missing in your organisation — this structured approach can reveal blind spots in current training needs analyses.

The use of two different frameworks suggests that literacy assessment outcomes vary by framework choice; select or develop assessment tools aligned with your specific AI capability goals rather than assuming one framework fits all contexts.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult employee AI literacy development requires translation of pedagogical principles to workplace settings.
takeaways: Structure AI literacy as part of a broader digital competency framework rather than in isolation — this holistic approach helps learners connect AI skills to existing digital and critical thinking capabilities.

Identify which foundational digital literacy skills (e.g., data interpretation, algorithmic reasoning) should precede AI-specific training to ensure employees have necessary prerequisites before advanced AI work.
Consider scaffolding AI competencies developmentally — employees at different stages of digital maturity may need different entry points and progression pathways into AI literacy.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development, likely US-based given Frontiers publication context. Applicability to other sectors and non-US contexts unclear without full text.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption is addressable through structured development programmes — design interventions that move educators from scepticism to practical readiness before expecting them to teach AI literacy.
Train-the-trainer approach may be essential in public health: develop AI capability in faculty first so they can credibly model and teach AI literacy to students and practitioners.
Embed AI literacy into existing public health curricula by having faculty co-design programmes rather than imposing external mandates — increases buy-in and relevance to domain-specific problems.

articles.title: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: High — systematic review methodology synthesises evidence across multiple studies and geographies, though the labour market contexts and data literacy definitions may vary by country and sector.
takeaways: Data literacy is increasingly framed as a core workplace competency; understanding how it's defined and measured across different labour markets can help you tailor development programs to your organisational context.
Systematic reviews of labour market skills often reveal gaps between what employers seek and what workers possess — identifying these gaps in your workforce can inform targeted upskilling priorities.

Data literacy encompasses both technical skills and critical interpretation abilities; training programs should balance hands-on tool use with conceptual understanding of data limitations and bias to build genuine capability.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses specifically on higher education context; applicability to corporate or other sectors would require adaptation of the four-domain model.
takeaways: Adopt a four-domain framework for structuring AI literacy programmes in your organisation: consider which domains (likely technical, ethical, strategic, and operational) your staff need to develop based on their roles.

Treat AI literacy as a meta-skill that enables learning of other capabilities, not just isolated technical knowledge — design learning pathways that help employees apply AI understanding across multiple business functions.
Use this model to audit existing L&D programmes: identify gaps in how you're developing AI capability across different knowledge domains rather than treating AI training as a single, one-off module.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition, which are not detailed in the snippet. Without information on participant demographics, sector, geography, or methodology, broad applicability cannot be assessed.
takeaways: AI-enabled work systems create dual pathways affecting employee wellbeing—some create strain (e.g. job insecurity, cognitive overload) while others provide resources (e.g. efficiency gains, skill development); organisations must actively manage both to prevent net negative outcomes.
When implementing AI tools, assess and mitigate strain factors (role clarity, autonomy, training support) alongside leveraging resource benefits to support employee mental health and engagement.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing populations and may not generalise to other healthcare roles or non-clinical sectors. Limited geographic scope information in snippet; generalisability further constrained by focus on medical AI implementation in healthcare settings.
takeaways: Preserve and actively protect work autonomy when implementing AI systems — nurses' wellbeing depends on maintaining control over decision-making, not just accepting AI tools. This suggests change management should emphasise how AI augments rather than replaces professional judgment.

Use AI readiness assessments as an early indicator of wellbeing risk; high readiness without autonomy safeguards may signal misalignment between organisational AI strategy and employee agency, warranting intervention before wellbeing deteriorates.

Design AI implementation with explicit autonomy protections built in — train staff on when to override AI recommendations, maintain final decision authority for high-stakes choices, and involve frontline workers in configuring AI workflows.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Findings reflect US workforce perspectives and may not fully generalise to Australian employment contexts, which have different labour regulations, industrial relations frameworks, and workplace cultures.
takeaways: Acknowledge worker uncertainty about AI-driven role changes explicitly in team conversations — psychological safety depends on managers naming the concern rather than avoiding it.
Design structured transition support (reskilling pathways, role clarity) to reduce anxiety-driven disengagement; uncertainty without a clear mitigation plan erodes both performance and retention.
Use organisational psychology principles to reframe AI adoption as collaborative rather than threatening — position employees as essential to implementation success, not as replaceable.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — appears to be a peer-reviewed empirical study, but geographic scope, sample size, sector, and methodology cannot be assessed from title and snippet provided.
takeaways: AI adoption in organizations has both positive and negative effects on employee creativity — leaders need to understand these dual mechanisms to design implementation strategies that maximize creative output rather than inadvertently constraining it.

Consider how your AI rollout might inadvertently reduce creative thinking (e.g., through over-standardization or reduced autonomy) and proactively design interventions to preserve or enhance creative problem-solving alongside efficiency gains.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability may be limited by focus on paternalistic leadership structures, which are more prevalent in certain cultural contexts (e.g., East Asian organisations) and may not reflect leadership dynamics in Western hierarchical models. Sample size and sector scope unclear from snippet.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customisation and adaptation decisions — this sense of ownership increases collaborative engagement with AI systems.

Recognise that paternalistic leadership (benevolent, directive guidance combined with employee care) can facilitate AI adoption; managers should balance clear AI implementation direction with genuine investment in employee wellbeing and skill development.
Implement 'AI crafting' opportunities — allowing employees to shape how AI tools fit their specific workflows — as a mechanism to bridge psychological ownership and active AI collaboration.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the snippet alone — the source appears to be a news summary rather than the original research article. Geographic scope, sample size, sector, and methodological details are not provided.
takeaways: Organisations implementing AI should prioritise psychological safety initiatives alongside adoption, as safety concerns may be a key mechanism linking AI introduction to negative mental health outcomes in staff.
Before deploying AI tools, assess and address employee concerns about job security, competence, and voice — this may buffer against depression and other adverse effects.
Consider measuring psychological safety as a leading indicator during AI rollout; declining safety scores may signal risk of employee mental health impacts that require intervention.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte report likely draws on client experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample details, geography, and methodological rigour are not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Shift focus from 'AI adoption' (technology rollout) to 'AI adaptation' (building capability and mindset change) — this reframing helps organisations prioritise behaviour change alongside technical implementation.

Design change programmes that explicitly target the human behaviours needed for AI success, not just feature training — this may include psychological safety, comfort with ambiguity, and willingness to upskill.
Use structured change approaches (rather than ad-hoc training) to systematically embed new ways of working; this increases the likelihood that teams will sustain and scale AI capability over time.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The theoretical framework (cognitive appraisal of stress and Job Demands-Resources perspective) is well-established, but application to AI awareness and job crafting may be context-dependent. Geographic scope unclear.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger job crafting through two distinct pathways: one via threat appraisal (stress response) and one via challenge appraisal (opportunity response). Organisations should monitor which pathway is dominant in their workforce and design interventions accordingly.

Frame AI implementation using challenge-appraisal language (skill development, new opportunities) rather than threat language (job loss, replacement) to encourage proactive job crafting rather than defensive stress responses.
Support job crafting explicitly after AI introduction—employees who reframe their role and reconfigure tasks independently show better adaptation than those left to navigate change passively.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical sample or geographic scope. Insights may reflect US academic/business context and may not directly transfer to Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption could support employee transitions rather than replace roles — frame capability development as an opportunity to upskill rather than a threat.

Design structured change management interventions that address both technical AI literacy and psychological readiness; resistance often stems from uncertainty rather than the technology itself, requiring clear communication about how roles will evolve.

articles.title: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be exploratory research identifying pathways to digital hoarding; generalisability depends on sample size and composition, which are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Digital hoarding in workplaces may have multiple distinct causes (e.g. anxiety about information loss, unclear deletion policies, organisational culture) rather than a single driver — interventions should diagnose the underlying pathway before addressing the behaviour.

Understanding whether employees hoard digital files due to risk aversion, lack of trust in systems, or unclear governance can help you design targeted behaviour-change initiatives (e.g. training, policy clarity, or system redesign) rather than generic 'clean up your files' campaigns.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis draws on global client work and industry trends, but reflects consulting firm perspective and may overrepresent large enterprises; applicability varies by organisation size and sector.
takeaways: Map your organisation's AI journey across three distinct horizons (near-term adoption, medium-term scaling, long-term transformation) to clarify which capability-building and behaviour-change efforts are most urgent for your stage.

Align employee upskilling interventions with your horizon timeline — near-term adoption requires rapid hands-on familiarity with tools, while long-term transformation demands deeper strategic thinking and risk literacy across leadership.
Use the three-horizon framework to communicate AI change roadmap to staff, reducing anxiety by showing concrete milestones and clarifying what 'impact' means for different roles and timeframes.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and organisational context, which are not detailed in the snippet. The approach-avoidance framework may apply broadly to AI adoption contexts, but findings could be limited by specific industry, geography, or organisational characteristics not mentioned.
takeaways: Monitor how employees respond to AI implementation—some may proactively reshape their roles (approach behaviours) while others may withdraw or resist (avoidance behaviours). Understanding this variation helps tailor change management strategies.

Use the approach-avoidance lens to design AI adoption interventions: foster approach-oriented job crafting by clearly communicating how AI augments (rather than replaces) employee skills, and address avoidance by providing upskilling opportunities and psychological safety during transition.

Assess your workforce's job crafting responses post-AI adoption to identify at-risk groups retreating from new tools, enabling early intervention through targeted support, mentoring, or reframing around opportunity rather than threat.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline coverage of research findings without access to original study methodology, sample characteristics, or effect sizes; generalisability depends on the underlying research design.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, rivalry-focused) may paradoxically attract romantic partners in short-term contexts, contrary to the intuition that narcissistic traits repel.

The finding highlights a puzzling gap between what we think attracts people and what actually does — personality traits associated with exploitation and coldness can still trigger romantic interest, at least initially.

This challenges the 'halo effect' assumption that people always prefer genuinely kind partners, suggesting attraction involves competing desires (stability vs. excitement, authenticity vs. status signalling).

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven news summaries typically lack methodological detail, sample size information, or geographic specificity needed to assess generalisability. The original research methodology cannot be determined from this snippet alone.
takeaways: Neuroimaging studies continue to reveal structural or functional brain differences associated with antisocial personality traits, challenging the idea that psychopathy is purely behavioural.
The framing of findings as 'shocking' highlights how accessible neuroscience can capture public imagination—even when effect sizes or practical implications remain uncertain.
Brain imaging research on psychopathy raises interesting questions about the nature/nurture debate and whether biological differences drive behaviour or reflect it.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from title and snippet alone; likely limited to laboratory conditions with controlled 'surprising' stimuli, which may not reflect how memory works for genuinely unexpected real-world events.
takeaways: People's personalities shape which surprises they remember and which they forget—some personality types may be 'surprise detectives' while others let unexpected moments slip away.
The counterintuitive bit: being surprised doesn't automatically make something memorable; how your personality is wired matters just as much as the shock factor itself.
Raises a fun question for everyday life: if you and a friend witness the same weird thing, your different personalities might mean you literally remember different versions of what happened.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on twin study sample composition and country of origin (not stated in snippet). Twin studies typically assume equal environments for identical and fraternal twins, which may not hold in all contexts.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs appear to have a measurable genetic component alongside environmental influences — challenging the assumption that such views are purely learned or ideologically chosen.

Twin studies reveal that personality traits and values linked to authoritarianism (like preference for order and hierarchy) may be partly heritable, suggesting political ideology isn't just a rational choice but rooted in psychological predisposition.

Understanding the nature/nurture split in authoritarianism helps explain why people across cultures and families can hold similar political worldviews — it's not just social contagion or family indoctrination.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings suggest cross-cultural consistency in the relationship between personality and music taste, though specific genres and cultural contexts may vary.
takeaways: Your taste in music genuinely reflects your personality type in predictable ways, and this pattern holds up across wildly different cultures and countries — it's not just a Western phenomenon.
The link between who you are and what you listen to is so strong and universal that it challenges the idea that music preferences are purely learned or culturally determined.
This suggests music might be a surprisingly honest 'personality fingerprint' — more revealing than you might think, whether someone's into heavy metal, classical, or pop.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — depends on sample size and diversity of wine reviewers analysed. Findings may reflect English-language wine review conventions rather than universal personality patterns.
takeaways: AI can detect personality traits from writing style in unexpected domains — what you say about wine reveals something about who you are.
Language patterns in subjective, passion-driven contexts (like wine tasting) may encode personality more clearly than formal writing, making them a quirky window into human nature.
The intersection of AI analysis and cultural taste preferences is ripe for playful discovery — there's probably a 'wine personality type' hiding in your tasting notes.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad applicability across geographies and sectors, though PwC's client base may skew toward larger organisations and professional services. Sample composition and methodology not detailed in snippet, limiting assessment of representativeness.
takeaways: Use survey findings on workforce concerns to identify which psychological safety risks are most salient to your employees—fears about job security, AI displacement, or management trust—and prioritise interventions accordingly.

Compare your organisation's safety culture against global benchmarks in the survey to identify gaps; consider whether employees' hopes (career development, flexibility, transparent leadership) are being met through your current policies and team practices.

Segment survey insights by role, tenure, or team to surface which groups may feel least psychologically safe, then design targeted conversations or structural changes to address their specific fears and build trust.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — likely based on a specific sample (geographic location and sector unclear from snippet), but addresses universal constructs (inclusive leadership, psychological safety, innovation) applicable across contexts.
takeaways: Inclusive leadership directly strengthens psychological safety within teams, creating the conditions necessary for innovation — leaders should actively solicit input from all team members and demonstrate genuine openness to diverse perspectives.

A leader's power distance orientation (tendency to accept hierarchical authority structures) moderates how effective inclusive leadership is; leaders who reduce perceived power distance see greater innovation benefits from their inclusive practices.

To maximise innovation outcomes, leaders should combine inclusive behaviours (valuing all voices) with a deliberate reduction of formal hierarchy — this combination creates safer environments where people feel able to experiment and challenge ideas.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology. Findings depend on sample characteristics (sector, geography, organisation size), measurement scales used, and whether results hold across different cultural contexts and AI implementation contexts.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent attention to psychological safety may increase depression risk — leaders should actively foster psychological safety (e.g., encouraging voice, normalising experimentation, protecting from blame) before and during AI rollouts.

Ethical leadership during AI adoption matters: transparent communication about AI's purpose, limits, and impact on roles; fair decision-making about AI use; and modelling integrity reduce the negative psychological effects on employees.

Monitor employee wellbeing proactively during AI transitions through regular check-ins and psychological safety surveys, rather than assuming technological change is neutral—depression and withdrawal may indicate unaddressed safety concerns.

articles.title: Team Dynamics Weaken When Employees Turn to AI instead of Colleagues - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Team Dynamics Weaken When Employees Turn to AI instead of Colleagues  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — presents conceptual argument about AI adoption risks without empirical data. Findings may not generalise across different organisational cultures, team structures, or AI implementation contexts.
takeaways: Design AI adoption policies that explicitly encourage peer collaboration alongside AI use — e.g. mandatory team check-ins, shared problem-solving sessions, or rotating decision-making to prevent over-reliance on AI and maintain interpersonal trust.

Monitor for erosion of psychological safety signals (e.g. reduced informal communication, decreased peer feedback) after introducing AI tools, as isolated AI use may weaken the social bonds necessary for team members to voice concerns or admit mistakes.

Create accountability structures where AI outputs are reviewed collaboratively rather than individually, preserving human dialogue and maintaining the relational foundations that enable team cohesion and psychological safety.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited — BCG report based on their consulting experience, likely with large multinational clients. Findings may not generalise to small-to-medium enterprises, public sector, or non-Western organisational contexts.
takeaways: Create explicit team norms that invite questions, dissent, and experimentation without fear of embarrassment or retribution — this removes barriers that prevent quieter or junior employees from contributing fully.

Measure psychological safety alongside performance metrics to identify teams where it is weak, then intervene by modelling vulnerability from leaders and establishing clear consequences for dismissive behaviour.

Use psychological safety as a lever to close equity gaps: when employees feel safe to speak up, underrepresented groups are more likely to voice ideas and concerns, leading to better decision-making and retention.

articles.title: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — conceptual framework from MIT Sloan likely reflects practices in knowledge-intensive sectors and large organisations, but applicability to smaller teams, different industries, or non-Western contexts is unclear.
takeaways: Create explicit norms where team members are expected to voice dissenting views and challenge assumptions without fear of retaliation — intellectual honesty requires psychological safety to function.
Design review processes and decision-making forums that reward critical thinking and the surfacing of problems early, not just consensus-seeking, to prevent groupthink from stifling innovation.
Model intellectual honesty visibly as a leader by admitting uncertainty, changing your mind when presented with evidence, and treating challenges to your ideas as valuable rather than threatening.
